items.title: Allan Jaffe Interview, 1969-04-16
items.q: Sandy, you know, more or less said that she would, you know, collect and that myself, you know, would try to

ctx.x: All right, today is April 16th, 1969, and I'm interviewing Alan Jaffe. Okay, Alan, could you tell me the story about how Preservation Hall started? Larry, Larry Borson had sessions in the hall, and was in his art gallery, associated artists, and I think about five years, going back to about 19, I think it was 1955 or 7, somewhere around there, where he started having Punch come over and play. Kid Thomas was playing there, and the Bazooka Trio used to play in Power of Ryan, and Patio, and they used to come over…
Do you think she really picked up my stupid thing? I don't know.

items.title: Betty Lee Hanson, Joe James, George Lewis, Joe Lewis, Joe Butler, Kid Thomas Valentine, Bill Russell, Allan…
items.q: Well, Alan was a big jazz fan, and I knew a little bit about it

ctx.x: Oh yes, it seemed to be something definitely developed in America, and I'm ready to believe from what I've seen and heard, that most of the better bands did originate here. Right in New Orleans. Right in New Orleans. There's been just entirely too many musicians here to say that, well, it's probably just the ones you heard of here. The ones that became famous happened to be born here, but there were so many here compared to other cities. There was nothing to compare with them in the north where I was raised, in…

How'd you get the idea to come down here and start this New Orleans revival of jazz or work with it? Well, we didn't come down here for that specific purpose. We came down from Philadelphia in about April and thought we'd be hearing a lot of these musicians and a lot of this music. And we didn't. We knew a lot of these men were still alive, that bands like the Eureka and Young Tuxedo Brass bands were still organized, and they were not playing anywhere. The first time that we saw them was about a month later. We…

Well, really, when we started, there was a group of people involved in this person we rent from now, Larry Bornstein, had been running these sessions on an informal basis. That would be, I guess, for at least 10 years. The band would come in occasionally during the night when they weren't playing. He'd open up his gallery to them and pass the kitty and pay them in from that. Mr. Russell had been down here for quite a while doing research on the musicians. And a boy here from California by the name of Grayson…

items.title: Betty Lee Hanson, Joe James, George Lewis, Joe Lewis, Joe Butler, Kid Thomas Valentine, Bill Russell, Allan…
items.q: Well, each band, as my wife said, there are 20 and each one is different.

ctx.x: Were you able to discern which bands are better than others? I mean, do you sort of say to someone, thank you, we don't want you anymore? We haven't had to. In other words, they're all of a pretty good quality then.

Well, each band, as my wife said, there are 20 and each one is different. It's, the quality is certainly different. And I think the musical idea that the people are trying to get across is different also. There's range from Peter Boccage who plays a more subdued, a more quiet type music, quiet for jazz anyway. Maybe a little more sophisticated than a person, a kid Thomas. Yeah. Where a kid Thomas is, is a lot, maybe rougher, a lot more direct.
Well, Alan, do you, this music is very exciting music and do you ever have any trouble with the crowds pushing in, with the crowds creating a riot, anything like this? Sort of.
